The brothers are overtaken, searched from eldest to youngest, and the cup is found. They tear their clothes, fall before Joseph, and Judah confesses a guilt God has found out. Joseph will keep only the man with the cup and send the rest home in peace—the test of whether they will abandon Rachel’s other son as they once sold Joseph.
text: Genesis 44:1–17 Genesis After the feast, Joseph orders sacks filled and money returned—and his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s grain. The brothers are overtaken, searched from eldest to youngest, and the cup is found. They tear their clothes, fall before Joseph, and Judah confesses a guilt God has found out. Joseph will keep only the man with the cup and send the rest home in peace—the test of whether they will abandon Rachel’s other son as they once sold Joseph. Then he commanded the steward of his house, “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in the mouth of his sack, Genesis 44:1 and put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the sack of the youngest, with his money for the grain.” And he did as Joseph told him. Genesis 44:2 As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away with their donkeys. Genesis 44:3 They had gone only a short distance from the city. Now Joseph said to his steward, “Up, follow after the men, and when you overtake them, say to them, ‘Why have you repaid evil for good? Genesis 44:4 Is it not from this that my lord drinks, and by this that he practices divination? You have done evil in doing this.’” Genesis 44:5 When he overtook them, he spoke to them these words. Genesis 44:6 They said to him, “Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing! Genesis 44:7 Behold, the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord’s house? Genesis 44:8 Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord’s servants.” Genesis 44:9 He said, “Let it be as you say: he who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent.” Genesis 44:10 Then each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground, and each man opened his sack. Genesis 44:11 And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack. Genesis 44:12 Then they tore their clothes, and every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city. Genesis 44:13 When Judah and his brothers came to Joseph’s house, he was still there. They fell before him to the ground. Genesis 44:14 Joseph said to them, “What deed is this that you have done? Do you not know that a man like me can indeed practice divination?” Genesis 44:15 And Judah said, “What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants; behold, we are my lord’s servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found.” Genesis 44:16 But he said, “Far be it from me that I should do so! Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father.” Genesis 44:17

title: Genesis 44:18–34
context: Judah draws near and pleads: the old father, the dead brother, the boy whose life is bound up with Jacob’s. He recites Joseph’s own demand, Jacob’s fear of Sheol, and his pledge to bear the blame. Then he offers himself as servant in Benjamin’s place—the sale’s leader now standing in as substitute so the beloved son can go home.
text: Genesis 44:18–34 Genesis Judah draws near and pleads: the old father, the dead brother, the boy whose life is bound up with Jacob’s. He recites Joseph’s own demand, Jacob’s fear of Sheol, and his pledge to bear the blame. Then he offers himself as servant in Benjamin’s place—the sale’s leader now standing in as substitute so the beloved son can go home. Then Judah went up to him and said, “Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears, and let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself. Genesis 44:18 My lord asked his servants, saying, ‘Have you a father, or a brother?’ Genesis 44:19 And we said to my lord, ‘We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother’s children, and his father loves him.’ Genesis 44:20 Then you said to your servants, ‘Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.’ Genesis 44:21 We said to my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.’ Genesis 44:22 Then you said to your servants, ‘Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you shall not see my face again.’ Genesis 44:23 When we went back to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord. Genesis 44:24 And when our father said, ‘Go again, buy us a little food,’ Genesis 44:25 we said, ‘We cannot go down. If our youngest brother goes with us, then we will go down. For we cannot see the man’s face unless our youngest brother is with us.’ Genesis 44:26 Then your servant my father said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons. Genesis 44:27 One left me, and I said, “Surely he has been torn to pieces,” and I have never seen him since. Genesis 44:28 If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol.’ Genesis 44:29 Now therefore, as soon as I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us, then, as his life is bound up in the boy’s life, Genesis 44:30 as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol. Genesis 44:31 For your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I do not bring him back to you, then I shall bear the blame before my father all my life.’ Genesis 44:32 Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers. Genesis 44:33 For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I fear to see the evil that would find my father.” Genesis 44:34

title: Genesis 45:1–15
context: After Judah’s plea in chapter 44, Joseph can no longer keep the mask. He clears the room, weeps, and names himself to the brothers who sold him—then reads their crime through God’s sending to preserve life, and calls them near for reconciliation.
text: Genesis 45:1–15 Genesis After Judah’s plea in chapter 44, Joseph can no longer keep the mask. He clears the room, weeps, and names himself to the brothers who sold him—then reads their crime through God’s sending to preserve life, and calls them near for reconciliation. Then Joseph could not control himself before all those who stood by him. He cried, “Make everyone go out from me.” So no one stayed with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers. Genesis 45:1 And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it. Genesis 45:2 And Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence. Genesis 45:3 So Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” And they came near. And he said, “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt. Genesis 45:4 And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. Genesis 45:5 For the famine has been in the land these two years, and there are yet five years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. Genesis 45:6 And God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth, and to keep alive for you many survivors. Genesis 45:7 So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt. Genesis 45:8 Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, ‘Thus says your son Joseph, God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not tarry. Genesis 45:9 You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me, you and your children and your children’s children, and your flocks, your herds, and all that you have. Genesis 45:10 There I will provide for you, for there are yet five years of famine to come, so that you and your household, and all that you have, do not come to poverty.’ Genesis 45:11 And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you. Genesis 45:12 You must tell my father of all my honor in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here.” Genesis 45:13 Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck. Genesis 45:14 And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. After that his brothers talked with him. Genesis 45:15

title: Genesis 45:16–28
context: News of the brothers reaches Pharaoh, who stocks the invitation with wagons and the fat of the land. The sons of Israel go home; Jacob’s heart goes numb at the report, then revives at Joseph’s words and wagons, and Israel says it is enough: he will go and see his son.
text: Genesis 45:16–28 Genesis News of the brothers reaches Pharaoh, who stocks the invitation with wagons and the fat of the land. The sons of Israel go home; Jacob’s heart goes numb at the report, then revives at Joseph’s words and wagons, and Israel says it is enough: he will go and see his son. When the report was heard in Pharaoh’s house, “Joseph’s brothers have come,” it pleased Pharaoh and his servants. Genesis 45:16 And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Say to your brothers, ‘Do this: load your beasts and go back to the land of Canaan, Genesis 45:17 and take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land.’ Genesis 45:18 And you, Joseph, are commanded to say, ‘Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father, and come. Genesis 45:19 Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.’” Genesis 45:20 The sons of Israel did so. And Joseph gave them wagons, according to the command of Pharaoh, and gave them provisions for the journey. Genesis 45:21 To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes. Genesis 45:22 To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey. Genesis 45:23 Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, “Do not quarrel on the way.” Genesis 45:24 So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. Genesis 45:25 And they told him, “Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt.” And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them. Genesis 45:26 But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived. Genesis 45:27 And Israel said, “It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.” Genesis 45:28

title: Genesis 46:1–27
context: Israel sets out with all he has, sacrifices at Beersheba to the God of his father Isaac, and God speaks in visions of the night: do not be afraid to go down to Egypt; I will make you a great nation there; I myself will go down with you, bring you up again, and Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes. Then the household migrates, and the sons of Israel are listed by mothers—Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah—with Joseph’s two sons born in Egypt; all the persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt are seventy.
text: Genesis 46:1–27 Genesis Israel sets out with all he has, sacrifices at Beersheba to the God of his father Isaac, and God speaks in visions of the night: do not be afraid to go down to Egypt; I will make you a great nation there; I myself will go down with you, bring you up again, and Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes. Then the household migrates, and the sons of Israel are listed by mothers—Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah—with Joseph’s two sons born in Egypt; all the persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt are seventy. So Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. Genesis 46:1 And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, “Jacob, Jacob.” And he said, “Here I am.” Genesis 46:2 Then he said, “I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. Genesis 46:3 I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes.” Genesis 46:4 Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him. Genesis 46:5 They also took their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him, Genesis 46:6 his sons, and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters, and his sons’ daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt. Genesis 46:7 Now these are the names of the descendants of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, Genesis 46:8 and the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. Genesis 46:9 The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. Genesis 46:10 The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Genesis 46:11 The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan); and the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. Genesis 46:12 The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob, and Shimron. Genesis 46:13 The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. Genesis 46:14 These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah; altogether his sons and his daughters numbered thirty-three. Genesis 46:15 The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. Genesis 46:16 The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, with Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel. Genesis 46:17 These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter; and these she bore to Jacob—sixteen persons. Genesis 46:18 The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin. Genesis 46:19 And to Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, bore to him. Genesis 46:20 And the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. Genesis 46:21 These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob—fourteen persons in all. Genesis 46:22 The son of Dan: Hushim. Genesis 46:23 The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. Genesis 46:24 These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob—seven persons in all. Genesis 46:25 All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not including Jacob’s sons’ wives, were sixty-six persons in all. Genesis 46:26 And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy. Genesis 46:27

title: Genesis 46:28–34
context: Judah is sent ahead to Joseph to show the way to Goshen. Joseph appears, falls on Israel’s neck, and weeps a good while; Israel says he can now die, having seen Joseph’s face. Joseph then coaches the brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds and livestock keepers, so they may dwell in Goshen—every shepherd being an abomination to the Egyptians.
text: Genesis 46:28–34 Genesis Judah is sent ahead to Joseph to show the way to Goshen. Joseph appears, falls on Israel’s neck, and weeps a good while; Israel says he can now die, having seen Joseph’s face. Joseph then coaches the brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds and livestock keepers, so they may dwell in Goshen—every shepherd being an abomination to the Egyptians. He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen. Genesis 46:28 Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while. Genesis 46:29 Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.” Genesis 46:30 Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. Genesis 46:31 And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.’ Genesis 46:32 When Pharaoh calls you and says, ‘What is your occupation?’ Genesis 46:33 you shall say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,’ in order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.” Genesis 46:34

title: Genesis 47:1–12
context: After the reunion in chapter 46, Joseph presents his family to Pharaoh. Five brothers request Goshen as sojourners; Pharaoh grants the best of the land. Jacob blesses the king, names his life a 130-year sojourn, and Joseph settles and feeds the household in Rameses.
text: Genesis 47:1–12 Genesis After the reunion in chapter 46, Joseph presents his family to Pharaoh. Five brothers request Goshen as sojourners; Pharaoh grants the best of the land. Jacob blesses the king, names his life a 130-year sojourn, and Joseph settles and feeds the household in Rameses. So Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, “My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now in the land of Goshen.” Genesis 47:1 And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh. Genesis 47:2 Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” And they said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were.” Genesis 47:3 They said to Pharaoh, “We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen.” Genesis 47:4 Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and your brothers have come to you. Genesis 47:5 The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock.” Genesis 47:6 Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. Genesis 47:7 And Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How many are the days of the years of your life?” Genesis 47:8 And Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning.” Genesis 47:9 And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh. Genesis 47:10 Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. Genesis 47:11 And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents. Genesis 47:12

title: Genesis 47:13–26
context: While Israel eats in Goshen, the famine empties Egypt and Canaan of money, livestock, land, and finally personal freedom. Joseph buys all for Pharaoh, exempts priestly land, issues seed, and fixes a fifth as statute—the people calling it salvation even as they become servants.
text: Genesis 47:13–26 Genesis While Israel eats in Goshen, the famine empties Egypt and Canaan of money, livestock, land, and finally personal freedom. Joseph buys all for Pharaoh, exempts priestly land, issues seed, and fixes a fifth as statute—the people calling it salvation even as they become servants. Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished by reason of the famine. Genesis 47:13 And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house. Genesis 47:14 And when the money was all spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone.” Genesis 47:15 And Joseph answered, “Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone.” Genesis 47:16 So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year. Genesis 47:17 And when that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, “We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent. The herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land. Genesis 47:18 Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate.” Genesis 47:19 So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for all the Egyptians sold their fields, because the famine was severe on them. The land became Pharaoh's. Genesis 47:20 As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other. Genesis 47:21 Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance that Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land. Genesis 47:22 Then Joseph said to the people, “Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land. Genesis 47:23 And at the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves and your households, and as food for your little ones.” Genesis 47:24 And they said, “You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh.” Genesis 47:25 So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth; the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's. Genesis 47:26

title: Genesis 47:27–31
context: The famine policy ends; the camera returns to Israel in Goshen: possessions, fruitfulness, and Jacob’s remaining seventeen years. Near death he binds Joseph under oath not to bury him in Egypt but with the fathers, then bows on the bed.
text: Genesis 47:27–31 Genesis The famine policy ends; the camera returns to Israel in Goshen: possessions, fruitfulness, and Jacob’s remaining seventeen years. Near death he binds Joseph under oath not to bury him in Egypt but with the fathers, then bows on the bed. Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly. Genesis 47:27 And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years. Genesis 47:28 And when the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt, Genesis 47:29 but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying place.” He answered, “I will do as you have said.” Genesis 47:30 And he said, “Swear to me”; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed. Genesis 47:31

title: Genesis 48:1–7
context: Joseph hears that Jacob is ill and brings Manasseh and Ephraim. Israel sits up, recites El Shaddai’s Luz promise, and adopts the two Egyptian-born sons as his own—equal to Reuben and Simeon—then remembers Rachel’s burial on the way to Ephrath.
text: Genesis 48:1–7 Genesis Joseph hears that Jacob is ill and brings Manasseh and Ephraim. Israel sits up, recites El Shaddai’s Luz promise, and adopts the two Egyptian-born sons as his own—equal to Reuben and Simeon—then remembers Rachel’s burial on the way to Ephrath. After this, Joseph was told, "Behold, your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Genesis 48:1 And it was told to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to you." Then Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed. Genesis 48:2 And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me, Genesis 48:3 and said to me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.' Genesis 48:4 And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. Genesis 48:5 And the children that you fathered after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance. Genesis 48:6 As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)." Genesis 48:7

title: Genesis 48:8–22
context: Dim-eyed Israel blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands so the right rests on Ephraim the younger. Joseph protests firstborn custom; Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know.” The blessing names God as shepherd and redeeming angel, sets Ephraim before Manasseh, and pledges return to the fathers’ land.
text: Genesis 48:8–22 Genesis Dim-eyed Israel blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands so the right rests on Ephraim the younger. Joseph protests firstborn custom; Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know.” The blessing names God as shepherd and redeeming angel, sets Ephraim before Manasseh, and pledges return to the fathers’ land. When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?" Genesis 48:8 Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them." Genesis 48:9 Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them. Genesis 48:10 And Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also." Genesis 48:11 Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth. Genesis 48:12 And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near him. Genesis 48:13 And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands (for Manasseh was the firstborn). Genesis 48:14 And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, Genesis 48:15 the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys; and in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth." Genesis 48:16 When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head. Genesis 48:17 And Joseph said to his father, "Not this way, my father; since this one is the firstborn, put your right hand on his head." Genesis 48:18 But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." Genesis 48:19 So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh. Genesis 48:20 Then Israel said to Joseph, "Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers." Genesis 48:21 Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow." Genesis 48:22

title: Genesis 49:1–12
context: Dying Jacob gathers his sons to tell what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses preeminence; Simeon and Levi are divided for violence; Judah receives praise, the lion, the scepter, and the obedience of the peoples—the messianic hinge of the chapter.
text: Genesis 49:1–12 Genesis Dying Jacob gathers his sons to tell what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses preeminence; Simeon and Levi are divided for violence; Judah receives praise, the lion, the scepter, and the obedience of the peoples—the messianic hinge of the chapter. Then Jacob called his sons and said, “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in days to come. Genesis 49:1 “Assemble and listen, O sons of Jacob, listen to Israel your father. Genesis 49:2 “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power. Genesis 49:3 Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled it—he went up to my couch! Genesis 49:4 “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords. Genesis 49:5 Let my soul come not into their council; O my glory, be not joined to their company. For in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen. Genesis 49:6 Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. Genesis 49:7 “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you. Genesis 49:8 Judah is a lion's cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? Genesis 49:9 The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples. Genesis 49:10 Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes. Genesis 49:11 His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.” Genesis 49:12

title: Genesis 49:13–28
context: Jacob continues through Zebulun, Issachar, Dan (with a cry for the Lord’s salvation), Gad, Asher, Naphtali, a long blessing on attacked-yet-helped Joseph, and Benjamin the wolf. He then names the twelve tribes, assigns each a suitable blessing, and the speech turns toward burial at Machpelah.
text: Genesis 49:13–28 Genesis Jacob continues through Zebulun, Issachar, Dan (with a cry for the Lord’s salvation), Gad, Asher, Naphtali, a long blessing on attacked-yet-helped Joseph, and Benjamin the wolf. He then names the twelve tribes, assigns each a suitable blessing, and the speech turns toward burial at Machpelah. “Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be at Sidon. Genesis 49:13 “Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. Genesis 49:14 He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor. Genesis 49:15 “Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel. Genesis 49:16 Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a viper by the path, that bites the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward. Genesis 49:17 I wait for your salvation, O Lord. Genesis 49:18 “Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels. Genesis 49:19 “Asher's food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal delicacies. Genesis 49:20 “Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns. Genesis 49:21 “Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall. Genesis 49:22 The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely, Genesis 49:23 yet his bow remained unmoved; his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel), Genesis 49:24 by the God of your father who will help you, by the Almighty who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb. Genesis 49:25 The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of my parents, up to the bounties of the everlasting hills. May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers. Genesis 49:26 “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil.” Genesis 49:27 All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him. Genesis 49:28

title: Genesis 49:29–33
context: After blessing the twelve, Jacob commands burial with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah—the plot Abraham bought in Canaan—then draws up his feet and is gathered to his people.
text: Genesis 49:29–33 Genesis After blessing the twelve, Jacob commands burial with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah—the plot Abraham bought in Canaan—then draws up his feet and is gathered to his people. Then he commanded them and said to them, “I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, Genesis 49:29 in the cave that is in the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. Genesis 49:30 There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah— Genesis 49:31 the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites.” Genesis 49:32 When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people. Genesis 49:33

title: Genesis 5:1–20
context: After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “and he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people.
text: Genesis 5:1–20 Genesis After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “and he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people. This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Genesis 5:1 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created. Genesis 5:2 When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. Genesis 5:3 The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:4 Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died. Genesis 5:5 When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh. Genesis 5:6 Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:7 Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died. Genesis 5:8 When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan. Genesis 5:9 Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:10 Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died. Genesis 5:11 When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel. Genesis 5:12 Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:13 Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died. Genesis 5:14 When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared. Genesis 5:15 Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:16 Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died. Genesis 5:17 When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch. Genesis 5:18 Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:19 Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died. Genesis 5:20

title: Genesis 5:21–32
context: The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood.
text: Genesis 5:21–32 Genesis The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood. When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah. Genesis 5:21 Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:22 Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years. Genesis 5:23 Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Genesis 5:24 When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech. Genesis 5:25 Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:26 Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died. Genesis 5:27 When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son Genesis 5:28 and called his name Noah, saying, “Out of the ground that the Lord has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands.” Genesis 5:29 Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:30 Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died. Genesis 5:31 After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 5:32

title: Genesis 50:1–14
context: Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt.
text: Genesis 50:1–14 Genesis Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt. Then Joseph fell on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him. Genesis 50:1 And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel. Genesis 50:2 Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days. Genesis 50:3 And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying, Genesis 50:4 ‘My father made me swear, saying, “I am about to die: in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there shall you bury me.” Now therefore, let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.’” Genesis 50:5 And Pharaoh answered, “Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear.” Genesis 50:6 So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, Genesis 50:7 as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen. Genesis 50:8 And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company. Genesis 50:9 When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days. Genesis 50:10 When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan. Genesis 50:11 Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them, Genesis 50:12 for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. Genesis 50:13 After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father. Genesis 50:14

title: Genesis 50:15–26
context: After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus.
text: Genesis 50:15–26 Genesis After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus. When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him.” Genesis 50:15 So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father gave this command before he died: Genesis 50:16 ‘Say to Joseph, “Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ And now, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him. Genesis 50:17 His brothers also came and fell down before him and said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Genesis 50:18 But Joseph said to them, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? Genesis 50:19 As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. Genesis 50:20 So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones.” Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them. Genesis 50:21 So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father’s house. Joseph lived 110 years. Genesis 50:22 And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were counted as Joseph’s own. Genesis 50:23 And Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Genesis 50:24 Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.” Genesis 50:25 So Joseph died, being 110 years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt. Genesis 50:26

title: Genesis 6:1–8
context: As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.
text: Genesis 6:1–8 Genesis As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord. When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, Genesis 6:1 the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose. Genesis 6:2 Then the Lord said, “My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years.” Genesis 6:3 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown. Genesis 6:4 The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. Genesis 6:5 And the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart. Genesis 6:6 So the Lord said, “I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them.” Genesis 6:7 But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord. Genesis 6:8

title: Genesis 6:9–22
context: A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him.
text: Genesis 6:9–22 Genesis A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. Genesis 6:9 And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 6:10 Now the earth was corrupt in God’s sight, and the earth was filled with violence. Genesis 6:11 And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. Genesis 6:12 And God said to Noah, “I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Genesis 6:13 Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. Genesis 6:14 This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Genesis 6:15 Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks. Genesis 6:16 For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die. Genesis 6:17 But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. Genesis 6:18 And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Genesis 6:19 Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Genesis 6:20 Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them.” Genesis 6:21 Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him. Genesis 6:22

title: Genesis 7:1–16
context: The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in.
text: Genesis 7:1–16 Genesis The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in. Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation." Genesis 7:1 Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate, Genesis 7:2 and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth. Genesis 7:3 For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground." Genesis 7:4 And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him. Genesis 7:5 Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. Genesis 7:6 And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Genesis 7:7 Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, Genesis 7:8 two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah. Genesis 7:9 And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth. Genesis 7:10 In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. Genesis 7:11 And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights. Genesis 7:12 On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark, Genesis 7:13 they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature. Genesis 7:14 They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life. Genesis 7:15 And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in. Genesis 7:16

title: Genesis 7:17–24
context: Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days.
text: Genesis 7:17–24 Genesis Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days. The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth. Genesis 7:17 The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters. Genesis 7:18 And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. Genesis 7:19 The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep. Genesis 7:20 And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind. Genesis 7:21 Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died. Genesis 7:22 He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. Genesis 7:23 And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days. Genesis 7:24

title: Genesis 8:1–19
context: After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again.
text: Genesis 8:1–19 Genesis After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again. But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided. Genesis 8:1 The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained, Genesis 8:2 and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated, Genesis 8:3 and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Genesis 8:4 And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen. Genesis 8:5 At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made Genesis 8:6 and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth. Genesis 8:7 Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground. Genesis 8:8 But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him. Genesis 8:9 He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. Genesis 8:10 And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth. Genesis 8:11 Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore. Genesis 8:12 In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. Genesis 8:13 In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out. Genesis 8:14 Then God said to Noah, Genesis 8:15 “Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons’ wives with you.” Genesis 8:16 “Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.” Genesis 8:17 So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives with him. Genesis 8:18 Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark. Genesis 8:19

title: Genesis 8:20–22
context: Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living creature as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure.
text: Genesis 8:20–22 Genesis Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living creature as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure. Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. Genesis 8:20 And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.” Genesis 8:21 While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease. Genesis 8:22

title: Genesis 9:1–17
context: After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth.
text: Genesis 9:1–17 Genesis After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth. And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. Genesis 9:1 The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered. Genesis 9:2 Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything. Genesis 9:3 But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood. Genesis 9:4 And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. Genesis 9:5 “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. Genesis 9:6 And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it.” Genesis 9:7 Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, Genesis 9:8 “Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, Genesis 9:9 and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. Genesis 9:10 I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth.” Genesis 9:11 And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: Genesis 9:12 I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. Genesis 9:13 When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, Genesis 9:14 I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. Genesis 9:15 When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:16 God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:17

title: Genesis 9:18–29
context: Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes.
text: Genesis 9:18–29 Genesis Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes. The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.) Genesis 9:18 These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Genesis 9:19 Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. Genesis 9:20 He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Genesis 9:21 And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Genesis 9:22 Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness. Genesis 9:23 When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, Genesis 9:24 he said, “Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.” Genesis 9:25 He also said, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. Genesis 9:26 May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.” Genesis 9:27 After the flood Noah lived 350 years. Genesis 9:28 All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died. Genesis 9:29

title: Matthew 1:1–17
context: Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story.
text: Matthew 1:1–17 Matthew Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story. The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Matthew 1:1 Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, Matthew 1:2 and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, Matthew 1:3 and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, Matthew 1:4 and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, Matthew 1:5 and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, Matthew 1:6 and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, Matthew 1:7 and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, Matthew 1:8 and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, Matthew 1:9 and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, Matthew 1:10 and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. Matthew 1:11 And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, Matthew 1:12 and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, Matthew 1:13 and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, Matthew 1:14 and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, Matthew 1:15 and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. Matthew 1:16 So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. Matthew 1:17

title: Matthew 1:18–25
context: After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise.
text: Matthew 1:18–25 Matthew After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise. Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:18 And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. Matthew 1:19 But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:20 She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” Matthew 1:21 All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: Matthew 1:22 “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). Matthew 1:23 When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, Matthew 1:24 but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus. Matthew 1:25

title: Matthew 10:1–4
context: After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him.
text: Matthew 10:1–4 Matthew After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him. And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. Matthew 10:1 The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Matthew 10:2 Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Matthew 10:3 Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. Matthew 10:4

title: Matthew 10:16–23
context: Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté.
text: Matthew 10:16–23 Matthew Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté. “Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Matthew 10:16 Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, Matthew 10:17 and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. Matthew 10:18 When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. Matthew 10:19 For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Matthew 10:20 Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death, Matthew 10:21 and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. Matthew 10:22 When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Matthew 10:23

title: Matthew 10:24–33
context: Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father.
text: Matthew 10:24–33 Matthew Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father. “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. Matthew 10:24 It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household. Matthew 10:25 “So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. Matthew 10:26 What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. Matthew 10:27 And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Matthew 10:28 Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. Matthew 10:29 But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Matthew 10:30 Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. Matthew 10:31 So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, Matthew 10:32 but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 10:33

title: Matthew 10:34–39
context: Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond.
text: Matthew 10:34–39 Matthew Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond. “Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. Matthew 10:34 For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Matthew 10:35 And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. Matthew 10:36 Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Matthew 10:37 And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Matthew 10:38 Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Matthew 10:39

title: Matthew 10:40–42
context: The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; even a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent.
text: Matthew 10:40–42 Matthew The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; even a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent. “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Matthew 10:40 The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. Matthew 10:41 And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.” Matthew 10:42

title: Matthew 10:5–15
context: Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not cancel later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances.
text: Matthew 10:5–15 Matthew Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not cancel later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances. These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, Matthew 10:5 but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matthew 10:6 And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ Matthew 10:7 Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. Matthew 10:8 Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, Matthew 10:9 no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food. Matthew 10:10 And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. Matthew 10:11 As you enter the house, greet it. Matthew 10:12 And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. Matthew 10:13 And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. Matthew 10:14 Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. Matthew 10:15

title: Matthew 11:1–6
context: After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him.
text: Matthew 11:1–6 Matthew After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him. When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. Matthew 11:1 Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples Matthew 11:2 and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” Matthew 11:3 And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: Matthew 11:4 the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Matthew 11:5 And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” Matthew 11:6

title: Matthew 11:16–19
context: After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.
text: Matthew 11:16–19 Matthew After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, Matthew 11:16 “‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ Matthew 11:17 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ Matthew 11:18 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” Matthew 11:19

title: Matthew 11:20–24
context: After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities where most of His mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.
text: Matthew 11:20–24 Matthew After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities where most of His mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom. Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. Matthew 11:20 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Matthew 11:21 But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. Matthew 11:22 And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Matthew 11:23 But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.” Matthew 11:24

title: Matthew 11:25–27
context: After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving. He praises the Father—Lord of heaven and earth—for a revelatory will that hides kingdom truth from the self-wise and discloses it to “little children,” then speaks of the Son’s exclusive knowledge of the Father and of those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
text: Matthew 11:25–27 Matthew After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving.
