context: Jesus draws near Jerusalem from Bethphage and the Mount of Olives at the start of Passion Week. He enters the city as Zechariah’s humble King—hailed by crowds, soon to confront the temple—so that readers see royal claim and cross-bound purpose together.
text: Matthew 21:1–11 Matthew Jesus draws near Jerusalem from Bethphage and the Mount of Olives at the start of Passion Week. He enters the city as Zechariah’s humble King—hailed by crowds, soon to confront the temple—so that readers see royal claim and cross-bound purpose together. Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, Matthew 21:1 saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. Matthew 21:2 If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." Matthew 21:3 This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, Matthew 21:4 "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" Matthew 21:5 The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. Matthew 21:6 They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Matthew 21:7 Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Matthew 21:8 And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" Matthew 21:9 And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" Matthew 21:10 And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee." Matthew 21:11

title: Matthew 21:12–17
context: After entering Jerusalem as Zechariah’s King, Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out commerce, heals the blind and lame, and receives the children’s Hosanna—while priests and scribes grow indignant—so Passion Week begins with cleansing, mercy, and contested praise.
text: Matthew 21:12–17 Matthew After entering Jerusalem as Zechariah’s King, Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out commerce, heals the blind and lame, and receives the children’s Hosanna—while priests and scribes grow indignant—so Passion Week begins with cleansing, mercy, and contested praise. And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. Matthew 21:12 He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." Matthew 21:13 And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. Matthew 21:14 But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant, Matthew 21:15 and they said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?" Matthew 21:16 And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. Matthew 21:17

title: Matthew 21:18–22
context: The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, and teaches the marveling disciples about faith that does not doubt and prayer that receives—linking judgment on barren religion with a call to living trust.
text: Matthew 21:18–22 Matthew The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, and teaches the marveling disciples about faith that does not doubt and prayer that receives—linking judgment on barren religion with a call to living trust. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. Matthew 21:18 And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. Matthew 21:19 When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?" Matthew 21:20 And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. Matthew 21:21 And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith." Matthew 21:22

title: Matthew 21:23–27
context: Back in the temple, chief priests and elders challenge Jesus’ authority while He teaches. He answers with a question about John’s baptism; trapped between heaven’s claim and fear of the crowd, they plead ignorance—and He withholds further disclosure of His authority.
text: Matthew 21:23–27 Matthew Back in the temple, chief priests and elders challenge Jesus’ authority while He teaches. He answers with a question about John’s baptism; trapped between heaven’s claim and fear of the crowd, they plead ignorance—and He withholds further disclosure of His authority. And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Matthew 21:23 Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. Matthew 21:24 The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' Matthew 21:25 But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet." Matthew 21:26 So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things." Matthew 21:27

title: Matthew 21:28–32
context: Still answering the temple leaders, Jesus tells the parable of the two sons: one refuses then goes; the other agrees then stays away. Saying yes is not the same as doing the Father’s will—and surprising repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of those who refused John’s light.
text: Matthew 21:28–32 Matthew Still answering the temple leaders, Jesus tells the parable of the two sons: one refuses then goes; the other agrees then stays away. Saying yes is not the same as doing the Father’s will—and surprising repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of those who refused John’s light. "What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.' Matthew 21:28 And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. Matthew 21:29 And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I go, sir,' but did not go. Matthew 21:30 Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. Matthew 21:31 For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him." Matthew 21:32

title: Matthew 21:33–46
context: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants: a master plants a vineyard, leases it, and sends servants—then his son—for fruit. The tenants beat, kill, and finally murder the heir. Citing Psalm 118, Jesus warns that the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the kingdom will be taken from fruitless leaders and given to a people who produce its fruits.
text: Matthew 21:33–46 Matthew Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants: a master plants a vineyard, leases it, and sends servants—then his son—for fruit. The tenants beat, kill, and finally murder the heir. Citing Psalm 118, Jesus warns that the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the kingdom will be taken from fruitless leaders and given to a people who produce its fruits. "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. Matthew 21:33 When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. Matthew 21:34 And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Matthew 21:35 Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. Matthew 21:36 Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' Matthew 21:37 But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.' Matthew 21:38 And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Matthew 21:39 When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?" Matthew 21:40 They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Matthew 21:41 Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?" Matthew 21:42 Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. Matthew 21:43 And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him." Matthew 21:44 When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. Matthew 21:45 And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet. Matthew 21:46

title: Matthew 22:1–14
context: Still in the temple courts after the vineyard parable, Jesus answers hostile leaders with another kingdom parable: a royal wedding feast. Refusal, judgment, wide invitation, and the wedding garment press both the sincerity of the call and the seriousness of coming on the King’s terms.
text: Matthew 22:1–14 Matthew Still in the temple courts after the vineyard parable, Jesus answers hostile leaders with another kingdom parable: a royal wedding feast. Refusal, judgment, wide invitation, and the wedding garment press both the sincerity of the call and the seriousness of coming on the King’s terms. And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, Matthew 22:1 "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, Matthew 22:2 and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Matthew 22:3 Again he sent other servants, saying, 'Tell those who are invited, "See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."' Matthew 22:4 But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, Matthew 22:5 while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Matthew 22:6 The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. Matthew 22:7 Then he said to his servants, 'The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Matthew 22:8 Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find.' Matthew 22:9 And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. Matthew 22:10 "But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. Matthew 22:11 And he said to him, 'Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?' And he was speechless. Matthew 22:12 Then the king said to the attendants, 'Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.' Matthew 22:13 For many are called, but few are chosen." Matthew 22:14

title: Matthew 22:15–22
context: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax. His answer—“render to Caesar… and to God”—exposes bad faith, affirms civil duty without surrendering worship, and leaves opponents marveling as Passion Week tension rises.
text: Matthew 22:15–22 Matthew Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax. His answer—“render to Caesar… and to God”—exposes bad faith, affirms civil duty without surrendering worship, and leaves opponents marveling as Passion Week tension rises. Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. Matthew 22:15 And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Matthew 22:16 Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?" Matthew 22:17 But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Matthew 22:18 Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius. Matthew 22:19 And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" Matthew 22:20 They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Matthew 22:21 When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. Matthew 22:22

title: Matthew 22:23–33
context: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a levirate-marriage riddle to discredit life after death. Jesus corrects their view of the age to come, grounds hope in God’s power and the Scriptures, and silences them before the listening crowds.
text: Matthew 22:23–33 Matthew Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a levirate-marriage riddle to discredit life after death. Jesus corrects their view of the age to come, grounds hope in God’s power and the Scriptures, and silences them before the listening crowds. The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, Matthew 22:23 saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.' Matthew 22:24 Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. Matthew 22:25 So too the second and third, down to the seventh. Matthew 22:26 And last of all, the woman died. Matthew 22:27 In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her." Matthew 22:28 But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Matthew 22:29 For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. Matthew 22:30 And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: Matthew 22:31 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living." Matthew 22:32 And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. Matthew 22:33

title: Matthew 22:34–40
context: After Jesus silences the Sadducees, Pharisees test Him with the greatest-commandment question. He answers with whole-person love for God (Deut 6:5) and neighbor-love like self (Lev 19:18), hanging all the Law and the Prophets on these two.
text: Matthew 22:34–40 Matthew After Jesus silences the Sadducees, Pharisees test Him with the greatest-commandment question. He answers with whole-person love for God (Deut 6:5) and neighbor-love like self (Lev 19:18), hanging all the Law and the Prophets on these two. But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. Matthew 22:34 And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. Matthew 22:35 "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?" Matthew 22:36 And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. Matthew 22:37 This is the great and first commandment. Matthew 22:38 And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Matthew 22:39 On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets." Matthew 22:40

title: Matthew 22:41–46
context: Jesus turns the examination on the Pharisees: whose son is the Christ? Psalm 110:1 shows David calling the Messiah “Lord,” so the Son of David is more than a mere descendant. No one dares ask Him another question.
text: Matthew 22:41–46 Matthew Jesus turns the examination on the Pharisees: whose son is the Christ? Psalm 110:1 shows David calling the Messiah “Lord,” so the Son of David is more than a mere descendant. No one dares ask Him another question. Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, Matthew 22:41 saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David." Matthew 22:42 He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, Matthew 22:43 "'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet"'?" Matthew 22:44 If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" Matthew 22:45 And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions. Matthew 22:46

title: Matthew 23:1–12
context: Still in the temple courts during Passion Week, Jesus turns from sparring with leaders to address the crowds and His disciples. Before the seven woes, He names the scribes’ and Pharisees’ teaching seat, exposes hypocrisy and honor-seeking, and sets the church’s posture: one Teacher, one Father, greatness as service, exaltation through humility.
text: Matthew 23:1–12 Matthew Still in the temple courts during Passion Week, Jesus turns from sparring with leaders to address the crowds and His disciples. Before the seven woes, He names the scribes’ and Pharisees’ teaching seat, exposes hypocrisy and honor-seeking, and sets the church’s posture: one Teacher, one Father, greatness as service, exaltation through humility. Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, Matthew 23:1 "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, Matthew 23:2 so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. Matthew 23:3 They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. Matthew 23:4 They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, Matthew 23:5 and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues Matthew 23:6 and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. Matthew 23:7 But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. Matthew 23:8 And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Matthew 23:9 Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. Matthew 23:10 The greatest among you shall be your servant. Matthew 23:11 Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." Matthew 23:12

title: Matthew 23:13–15
context: After exposing honor-seeking religion, Jesus opens the seven woes. The first strike hypocrisy that blocks the kingdom and mission that multiplies ruin. (ESV omits v. 14, present in some manuscripts as a widows’-houses woe.)
text: Matthew 23:13–15 Matthew After exposing honor-seeking religion, Jesus opens the seven woes. The first strike hypocrisy that blocks the kingdom and mission that multiplies ruin. (ESV omits v. 14, present in some manuscripts as a widows’-houses woe.) "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. Matthew 23:13 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. Matthew 23:15

title: Matthew 23:16–22
context: Jesus continues the woes against casuistry that ranks oaths by gold and gifts while sidelining temple, altar, and God. Blind guides invent loopholes; He restores the sacred order that ends at the throne.
text: Matthew 23:16–22 Matthew Jesus continues the woes against casuistry that ranks oaths by gold and gifts while sidelining temple, altar, and God. Blind guides invent loopholes; He restores the sacred order that ends at the throne. "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' Matthew 23:16 You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? Matthew 23:17 And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' Matthew 23:18 You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? Matthew 23:19 So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. Matthew 23:20 And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. Matthew 23:21 And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it." Matthew 23:22

title: Matthew 23:23–28
context: Mid-woes: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness; cleaning cups and tombs while greed and lawlessness fill the inside. Jesus demands weightier obedience and inward purity, not cosmetic religion.
text: Matthew 23:23–28 Matthew Mid-woes: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness; cleaning cups and tombs while greed and lawlessness fill the inside. Jesus demands weightier obedience and inward purity, not cosmetic religion. "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. Matthew 23:23 You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! Matthew 23:24 "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. Matthew 23:25 You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. Matthew 23:26 "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. Matthew 23:27 So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness." Matthew 23:28

title: Matthew 23:29–36
context: Final woe: decorating prophets’ tombs while sharing the fathers’ murderous line. Jesus sends prophets, wise men, and scribes they will kill; righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah comes on this generation.
text: Matthew 23:29–36 Matthew Final woe: decorating prophets’ tombs while sharing the fathers’ murderous line. Jesus sends prophets, wise men, and scribes they will kill; righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah comes on this generation. "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, Matthew 23:29 saying, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.' Matthew 23:30 Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Matthew 23:31 Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. Matthew 23:32 You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Matthew 23:33 Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town, Matthew 23:34 so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Matthew 23:35 Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation." Matthew 23:36

title: Matthew 23:37–39
context: After the woes, Jesus laments Jerusalem: prophetic killers whom He longed to gather as a hen gathers her brood—yet they were not willing. The house is left desolate until the city blesses the Coming One.
text: Matthew 23:37–39 Matthew After the woes, Jesus laments Jerusalem: prophetic killers whom He longed to gather as a hen gathers her brood—yet they were not willing. The house is left desolate until the city blesses the Coming One. "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! Matthew 23:37 See, your house is left to you desolate. Matthew 23:38 For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'" Matthew 23:39

title: Matthew 24:1–14
context: Leaving the temple after the woes of chapter 23, Jesus predicts its total ruin. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask about timing, His coming, and the end of the age. He answers first with pastoral warnings: deception, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, cold love—and the gospel’s worldwide witness. These are birth pains, not yet the end; endurance and proclamation mark His people until the end comes.
text: Matthew 24:1–14 Matthew Leaving the temple after the woes of chapter 23, Jesus predicts its total ruin. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask about timing, His coming, and the end of the age. He answers first with pastoral warnings: deception, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, cold love—and the gospel’s worldwide witness. These are birth pains, not yet the end; endurance and proclamation mark His people until the end comes. Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. Matthew 24:1 But he answered them, "You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down." Matthew 24:2 As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" Matthew 24:3 And Jesus answered them, "See that no one leads you astray. Matthew 24:4 For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray. Matthew 24:5 And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. Matthew 24:6 For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places. Matthew 24:7 All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. Matthew 24:8 "Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake. Matthew 24:9 And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. Matthew 24:10 And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. Matthew 24:11 And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold. Matthew 24:12 But the one who endures to the end will be saved. Matthew 24:13 And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come. Matthew 24:14

title: Matthew 24:15–28
context: Still on Olivet, Jesus turns from birth pains to a sharper crisis: Daniel’s abomination in the holy place, urgent flight from Judea, unmatched tribulation shortened for the elect, and a fresh wave of false christs with signs. He tells them beforehand so they will not chase wilderness rumors or inner-room sightings. His own coming will be as public as lightning from east to west.
text: Matthew 24:15–28 Matthew Still on Olivet, Jesus turns from birth pains to a sharper crisis: Daniel’s abomination in the holy place, urgent flight from Judea, unmatched tribulation shortened for the elect, and a fresh wave of false christs with signs. He tells them beforehand so they will not chase wilderness rumors or inner-room sightings. His own coming will be as public as lightning from east to west. "So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), Matthew 24:15 then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Matthew 24:16 Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, Matthew 24:17 and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. Matthew 24:18 And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Matthew 24:19 Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath. Matthew 24:20 For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. Matthew 24:21 And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short. Matthew 24:22 Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. Matthew 24:23 For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. Matthew 24:24 See, I have told you beforehand. Matthew 24:25 So, if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out. If they say, 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it. Matthew 24:26 For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Matthew 24:27 Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather." Matthew 24:28

title: Matthew 24:29–31
context: After the tribulation of those days, Jesus describes cosmic shaking, the sign of the Son of Man, worldwide mourning, and His cloud-coming in power and glory. Angels with trumpet gather His elect from the four winds—public, royal, and final for the hope of His people.
text: Matthew 24:29–31 Matthew After the tribulation of those days, Jesus describes cosmic shaking, the sign of the Son of Man, worldwide mourning, and His cloud-coming in power and glory. Angels with trumpet gather His elect from the four winds—public, royal, and final for the hope of His people. "Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Matthew 24:29 Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. Matthew 24:30 And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other." Matthew 24:31

title: Matthew 24:32–35
context: Jesus adds the fig-tree lesson: tender branch and leaves mean summer is near; likewise “all these things” mean He is near, at the gates. He seals it with a solemn “Truly” about this generation and the unmatched permanence of His words over heaven and earth.
text: Matthew 24:32–35 Matthew Jesus adds the fig-tree lesson: tender branch and leaves mean summer is near; likewise “all these things” mean He is near, at the gates. He seals it with a solemn “Truly” about this generation and the unmatched permanence of His words over heaven and earth. "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. Matthew 24:32 So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates. Matthew 24:33 Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Matthew 24:34 Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." Matthew 24:35

title: Matthew 24:36–44
context: Jesus turns to the unknown day and hour: angels do not know it, nor the Son, but the Father only. The days of Noah picture ordinary life interrupted by sudden judgment. Separation scenes and a thief-in-the-night image press one charge—stay awake and be ready, for the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour.
text: Matthew 24:36–44 Matthew Jesus turns to the unknown day and hour: angels do not know it, nor the Son, but the Father only. The days of Noah picture ordinary life interrupted by sudden judgment. Separation scenes and a thief-in-the-night image press one charge—stay awake and be ready, for the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour. "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only. Matthew 24:36 For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Matthew 24:37 For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, Matthew 24:38 and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Matthew 24:39 Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. Matthew 24:40 Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left. Matthew 24:41 Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. Matthew 24:42 But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into. Matthew 24:43 Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect." Matthew 24:44

title: Matthew 24:45–51
context: Jesus closes the chapter with the faithful and wise servant set over the household to feed others in season, versus the wicked servant who assumes delay, abuses peers, and joins drunkards. Blessing and promotion meet the found-doing servant; sudden return, dismembering judgment, and hypocrites’ weeping meet the wicked one—bridge into chapter 25’s readiness parables.
text: Matthew 24:45–51 Matthew Jesus closes the chapter with the faithful and wise servant set over the household to feed others in season, versus the wicked servant who assumes delay, abuses peers, and joins drunkards. Blessing and promotion meet the found-doing servant; sudden return, dismembering judgment, and hypocrites’ weeping meet the wicked one—bridge into chapter 25’s readiness parables. "Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his master has set over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? Matthew 24:45 Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Matthew 24:46 Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. Matthew 24:47 But if that wicked servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' Matthew 24:48 and begins to beat his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards, Matthew 24:49 the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know Matthew 24:50 and will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Matthew 24:51

title: Matthew 25:1–13
context: Still answering the disciples’ watchfulness questions from chapter 24, Jesus pictures the kingdom as ten virgins awaiting a delayed bridegroom. Wisdom and folly turn on oil ready before the midnight cry; those prepared enter the feast, the door shuts, and the refrain returns: watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
text: Matthew 25:1–13 Matthew Still answering the disciples’ watchfulness questions from chapter 24, Jesus pictures the kingdom as ten virgins awaiting a delayed bridegroom. Wisdom and folly turn on oil ready before the midnight cry; those prepared enter the feast, the door shuts, and the refrain returns: watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour. Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Matthew 25:1 Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. Matthew 25:2 For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, Matthew 25:3 but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. Matthew 25:4 As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. Matthew 25:5 But at midnight there was a cry, 'Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.' Matthew 25:6 Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. Matthew 25:7 And the foolish said to the wise, 'Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.' Matthew 25:8 But the wise answered, saying, 'Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.' Matthew 25:9 And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. Matthew 25:10 Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, 'Lord, lord, open to us.' Matthew 25:11 But he answered, 'Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.' Matthew 25:12 Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour. Matthew 25:13

title: Matthew 25:14–30
context: Jesus continues the readiness theme with a journeying master who entrusts unequal talents according to ability, then returns after a long time to settle accounts. Faithful servants enter the master’s joy; the fearful, idle servant loses even what he hid and is cast into outer darkness—stewardship under delayed return.
text: Matthew 25:14–30 Matthew Jesus continues the readiness theme with a journeying master who entrusts unequal talents according to ability, then returns after a long time to settle accounts. Faithful servants enter the master’s joy; the fearful, idle servant loses even what he hid and is cast into outer darkness—stewardship under delayed return. For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. Matthew 25:14 To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away. Matthew 25:15 He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. Matthew 25:16 So also he who had the two talents made two talents more. Matthew 25:17 But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master's money. Matthew 25:18 Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. Matthew 25:19 And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.' Matthew 25:20 His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' Matthew 25:21 And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.' Matthew 25:22 His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' Matthew 25:23 He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, 'Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed, Matthew 25:24 so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.' Matthew 25:25 But his master answered him, 'You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed? Matthew 25:26 Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. Matthew 25:27 So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. Matthew 25:28 For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Matthew 25:29 And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.' Matthew 25:30

title: Matthew 25:31–46
context: Jesus ends the discourse with the Son of Man in glory, angels, and a throne of judgment over all nations. Sheep and goats are separated; the King identifies with ‘the least of these’ in hunger, thirst, strangerhood, nakedness, sickness, and prison. Eternal punishment and eternal life close the chapter—mercy’s fruit revealed, not a rival gospel.
text: Matthew 25:31–46 Matthew Jesus ends the discourse with the Son of Man in glory, angels, and a throne of judgment over all nations. Sheep and goats are separated; the King identifies with ‘the least of these’ in hunger, thirst, strangerhood, nakedness, sickness, and prison. Eternal punishment and eternal life close the chapter—mercy’s fruit revealed, not a rival gospel. When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Matthew 25:31 Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. Matthew 25:32 And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left. Matthew 25:33 Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Matthew 25:34 For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, Matthew 25:35 I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.' Matthew 25:36 Then the righteous will answer him, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? Matthew 25:37 And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? Matthew 25:38 And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?' Matthew 25:39 And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.' Matthew 25:40 Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Matthew 25:41 For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink, Matthew 25:42 I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.' Matthew 25:43 Then they also will answer, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?' Matthew 25:44 Then he will answer them, saying, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.' Matthew 25:45 And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." Matthew 25:46

title: Matthew 26:1–5
context: After the Olivet Discourse (chs. 24–25), Matthew opens the Passion narrative. Jesus announces that Passover is two days away and that the Son of Man will be delivered up to crucifixion, while the chief priests and elders plot a stealthy arrest—yet delay it for fear of the people.
text: Matthew 26:1–5 Matthew After the Olivet Discourse (chs. 24–25), Matthew opens the Passion narrative. Jesus announces that Passover is two days away and that the Son of Man will be delivered up to crucifixion, while the chief priests and elders plot a stealthy arrest—yet delay it for fear of the people. When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, Matthew 26:1 “You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” Matthew 26:2 Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, Matthew 26:3 and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him. Matthew 26:4 But they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” Matthew 26:5

title: Matthew 26:14–16
context: Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests, bargains to deliver Jesus for silver, and from then on seeks an opportunity to betray Him.
text: Matthew 26:14–16 Matthew Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests, bargains to deliver Jesus for silver, and from then on seeks an opportunity to betray Him. Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests Matthew 26:14 and said, “What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?” And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. Matthew 26:15 And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him. Matthew 26:16

title: Matthew 26:17–25
context: On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus directs them to a certain man in the city; they prepare the meal. At table He announces that one of them will betray Him, identifies the traitor by the dipped morsel exchange with Judas, and Judas answers with a feigned question.
text: Matthew 26:17–25 Matthew On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus directs them to a certain man in the city; they prepare the meal. At table He announces that one of them will betray Him, identifies the traitor by the dipped morsel exchange with Judas, and Judas answers with a feigned question. Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?” Matthew 26:17 He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” Matthew 26:18 And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. Matthew 26:19 When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. Matthew 26:20 And as they were eating, he said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” Matthew 26:21 And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, “Is it I, Lord?” Matthew 26:22 He answered, “He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. Matthew 26:23 The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” Matthew 26:24 Judas, who would betray him, answered, “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said so.” Matthew 26:25

title: Matthew 26:26–30
context: During the Passover meal Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper: bread as His body, the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. He points ahead to drinking new with them in His Father’s kingdom, then they sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.)
text: Matthew 26:26–30 Matthew During the Passover meal Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper: bread as His body, the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. He points ahead to drinking new with them in His Father’s kingdom, then they sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.) Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” Matthew 26:26 And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you, Matthew 26:27 for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. Matthew 26:28 I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” Matthew 26:29 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Matthew 26:30

title: Matthew 26:31–35
context: On the way Jesus cites Zechariah: the shepherd will be struck and the sheep scattered, yet promises to go before them to Galilee after He is raised. Peter vows loyalty even to death; Jesus foretells a threefold denial before the rooster crows; the others echo Peter’s boast.
text: Matthew 26:31–35 Matthew On the way Jesus cites Zechariah: the shepherd will be struck and the sheep scattered, yet promises to go before them to Galilee after He is raised. Peter vows loyalty even to death; Jesus foretells a threefold denial before the rooster crows; the others echo Peter’s boast. Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ Matthew 26:31 But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” Matthew 26:32 Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.” Matthew 26:33 Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Matthew 26:34 Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!” And all the disciples said the same. Matthew 26:35

title: Matthew 26:36–46
context: At Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James, and John aside, grieves to the point of death, and thrice prays that the cup pass if possible—yet submits to the Father’s will. The disciples sleep despite His call to watch and pray; He returns the third time announcing the hour and the betrayer’s arrival. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.)
text: Matthew 26:36–46 Matthew At Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James, and John aside, grieves to the point of death, and thrice prays that the cup pass if possible—yet submits to the Father’s will. The disciples sleep despite His call to watch and pray; He returns the third time announcing the hour and the betrayer’s arrival. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.) Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go over there and pray.” Matthew 26:36 And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. Matthew 26:37 Then he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me.” Matthew 26:38 And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Matthew 26:39 And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, “So, could you not watch with me one hour? Matthew 26:40 Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Matthew 26:41 Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” Matthew 26:42 And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. Matthew 26:43 So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. Matthew 26:44 Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Matthew 26:45 Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” Matthew 26:46

title: Matthew 26:47–56
context: Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders, betrays Jesus with a kiss, and the arrest follows. A disciple strikes with the sword; Jesus rebukes violence, affirms He could call legions of angels, and submits so the Scriptures are fulfilled. The disciples flee.
text: Matthew 26:47–56 Matthew Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders, betrays Jesus with a kiss, and the arrest follows. A disciple strikes with the sword; Jesus rebukes violence, affirms He could call legions of angels, and submits so the Scriptures are fulfilled. The disciples flee. While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. Matthew 26:47 Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man; seize him.” Matthew 26:48 And he came up to Jesus at once and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” And he kissed him. Matthew 26:49 Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you came to do.” Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. Matthew 26:50 And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Matthew 26:51 Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Matthew 26:52 Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? Matthew 26:53 But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?” Matthew 26:54 At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. Matthew 26:55 But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. Matthew 26:56

title: Matthew 26:57–68
context: Jesus is led to Caiaphas; the scribes and elders gather. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard. The council seeks false testimony, finally charges Jesus under the temple saying and His confession as the Christ, the Son of God. The high priest declares blasphemy; they condemn Him as deserving death and begin to mock and strike Him.
text: Matthew 26:57–68 Matthew Jesus is led to Caiaphas; the scribes and elders gather. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard. The council seeks false testimony, finally charges Jesus under the temple saying and His confession as the Christ, the Son of God. The high priest declares blasphemy; they condemn Him as deserving death and begin to mock and strike Him. Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. Matthew 26:57 And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end. Matthew 26:58 Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, Matthew 26:59 but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward Matthew 26:60 and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.’” Matthew 26:61 And the high priest stood up and said, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” Matthew 26:62 But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Matthew 26:63 Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” Matthew 26:64 Then the high priest tore his robes and said, “He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. Matthew 26:65 What is your judgment?” They answered, “He deserves death.” Matthew 26:66 Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, Matthew 26:67 saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” Matthew 26:68

title: Matthew 26:6–13
context: While leaders plot in Jerusalem, Jesus is at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper. A woman anoints Him with costly ointment; the disciples call it waste; Jesus defends her act as beautiful preparation for His burial and promises that the gospel will remember her wherever it is proclaimed.
text: Matthew 26:6–13 Matthew While leaders plot in Jerusalem, Jesus is at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper. A woman anoints Him with costly ointment; the disciples call it waste; Jesus defends her act as beautiful preparation for His burial and promises that the gospel will remember her wherever it is proclaimed. Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, Matthew 26:6 a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table. Matthew 26:7 And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? Matthew 26:8 For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.” Matthew 26:9 But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. Matthew 26:10 For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. Matthew 26:11 In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial. Matthew 26:12 Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” Matthew 26:13

title: Matthew 26:69–75
context: In the courtyard a servant girl, then another, then bystanders confront Peter about being with Jesus. He denies with oath and curse that he does not know the man. The rooster crows; Peter remembers Jesus’ word, goes out, and weeps bitterly.
text: Matthew 26:69–75 Matthew In the courtyard a servant girl, then another, then bystanders confront Peter about being with Jesus. He denies with oath and curse that he does not know the man. The rooster crows; Peter remembers Jesus’ word, goes out, and weeps bitterly. Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” Matthew 26:69 But he denied it before them all, saying, “I do not know what you mean.” Matthew 26:70 And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” Matthew 26:71 And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” Matthew 26:72 After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you.” Matthew 26:73 Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know the man.” And immediately the rooster crowed. Matthew 26:74 And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went out and wept bitterly. Matthew 26:75

title: Matthew 27:1–2
context: After the night trial and Peter’s denial (ch. 26), morning comes. The chief priests and elders take formal counsel to put Jesus to death, then bind Him and deliver Him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.
text: Matthew 27:1–2 Matthew After the night trial and Peter’s denial (ch. 26), morning comes. The chief priests and elders take formal counsel to put Jesus to death, then bind Him and deliver Him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. Matthew 27:1 And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor. Matthew 27:2

title: Matthew 27:11–14
context: Bound and delivered to Pilate (vv. 1–2), Jesus now stands before the Roman governor. Pilate asks about kingship; the chief priests and elders heap accusations; Jesus answers little, and the governor is greatly amazed.
text: Matthew 27:11–14 Matthew Bound and delivered to Pilate (vv. 1–2), Jesus now stands before the Roman governor. Pilate asks about kingship; the chief priests and elders heap accusations; Jesus answers little, and the governor is greatly amazed. Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You have said so.” Matthew 27:11 But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer. Matthew 27:12 Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” Matthew 27:13 But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed. Matthew 27:14

title: Matthew 27:15–26
context: After Jesus’ silence before Pilate (vv. 11–14), the feast custom of releasing a prisoner sets the stage. Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus; the crowd, stirred by the priests, chooses Barabbas and demands crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, the people accept bloodguilt, and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified.
text: Matthew 27:15–26 Matthew After Jesus’ silence before Pilate (vv. 11–14), the feast custom of releasing a prisoner sets the stage. Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus; the crowd, stirred by the priests, chooses Barabbas and demands crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, the people accept bloodguilt, and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified. Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. Matthew 27:15 And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Matthew 27:16 So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” Matthew 27:17 For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up. Matthew 27:18 Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream.” Matthew 27:19 Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. Matthew 27:20 The governor again said to them, “Which of the two do you want me to release for you?” And they said, “Barabbas.” Matthew 27:21 Pilate said to them, “Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said, “Let him be crucified!” Matthew 27:22 And he said, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Let him be crucified!” Matthew 27:23 So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves.” Matthew 27:24 And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” Matthew 27:25 Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified. Matthew 27:26

title: Matthew 27:27–31
context: After Barabbas is released and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified (v. 26), the governor’s soldiers take Jesus into the headquarters, mock His kingship with robe, thorns, and reed, then lead Him away to the cross.
text: Matthew 27:27–31 Matthew After Barabbas is released and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified (v. 26), the governor’s soldiers take Jesus into the headquarters, mock His kingship with robe, thorns, and reed, then lead Him away to the cross. Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. Matthew 27:27 And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, Matthew 27:28 and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” Matthew 27:29 And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head. Matthew 27:30 And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him. Matthew 27:31

title: Matthew 27:3–10
context: As Jesus is condemned and handed to Pilate, Judas the betrayer is seized with remorse, returns the silver, and dies in despair; the priests buy the potter’s field, and Matthew records Scripture’s fulfillment.
text: Matthew 27:3–10 Matthew As Jesus is condemned and handed to Pilate, Judas the betrayer is seized with remorse, returns the silver, and dies in despair; the priests buy the potter’s field, and Matthew records Scripture’s fulfillment. Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, Matthew 27:3 saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” They said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” Matthew 27:4 And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. Matthew 27:5 But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money.” Matthew 27:6 So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Matthew 27:7 Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. Matthew 27:8 Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, Matthew 27:9 and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me.” Matthew 27:10

title: Matthew 27:32–44
context: On the way to Golgotha Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified between robbers, titled King of the Jews, and mocked by passersby and leaders who dare Him to come down from the cross.
text: Matthew 27:32–44 Matthew On the way to Golgotha Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified between robbers, titled King of the Jews, and mocked by passersby and leaders who dare Him to come down from the cross. As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross. Matthew 27:32 And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), Matthew 27:33 they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it. Matthew 27:34 And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Matthew 27:35 Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. Matthew 27:36 And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” Matthew 27:37 Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left. Matthew 27:38 And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads Matthew 27:39 and saying, “You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” Matthew 27:40 So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, Matthew 27:41 “He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. Matthew 27:42 He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” Matthew 27:43 And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way. Matthew 27:44

title: Matthew 27:45–56
context: From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covers the land. Jesus cries the forsaken cry of Psalm 22, yields up His spirit, the temple curtain tears, earth shakes, saints are raised, and a centurion confesses the Son of God while women watch from a distance.
text: Matthew 27:45–56 Matthew From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covers the land. Jesus cries the forsaken cry of Psalm 22, yields up His spirit, the temple curtain tears, earth shakes, saints are raised, and a centurion confesses the Son of God while women watch from a distance. Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. Matthew 27:45 And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Matthew 27:46 And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.” Matthew 27:47 And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink. Matthew 27:48 But the others said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.” Matthew 27:49 And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. Matthew 27:50 And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. Matthew 27:51 The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised, Matthew 27:52 and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. Matthew 27:53 When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, “Truly this was the Son of God!” Matthew 27:54 There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, Matthew 27:55 among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Matthew 27:56

title: Matthew 27:57–61
context: Evening falls. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new rock tomb; Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite, watching.
text: Matthew 27:57–61 Matthew Evening falls. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new rock tomb; Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite, watching. When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. Matthew 27:57 He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him. Matthew 27:58 And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud Matthew 27:59 and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away. Matthew 27:60 Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. Matthew 27:61

title: Matthew 27:62–66
context: After Preparation Day, chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb against a stolen-body story. Pilate grants a guard; they seal the stone—unwittingly strengthening the later witness of resurrection.
text: Matthew 27:62–66 Matthew After Preparation Day, chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb against a stolen-body story. Pilate grants a guard; they seal the stone—unwittingly strengthening the later witness of resurrection. The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate Matthew 27:62 and said, “Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’ Matthew 27:63 Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, ‘He has risen from the dead,’ and the last fraud will be worse than the first.” Matthew 27:64 Pilate said to them, “You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can.” Matthew 27:65 So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard. Matthew 27:66

title: Matthew 28:1–10
context: At dawn on the first day of the week the women come to the tomb. An angel of the Lord rolls back the stone, announces that Jesus has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples. As they go, the risen Jesus meets them; they worship Him, and He directs them—and His brothers—to Galilee.
text: Matthew 28:1–10 Matthew At dawn on the first day of the week the women come to the tomb. An angel of the Lord rolls back the stone, announces that Jesus has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples. As they go, the risen Jesus meets them; they worship Him, and He directs them—and His brothers—to Galilee. Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. Matthew 28:1 And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it. Matthew 28:2 His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. Matthew 28:3 And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men. Matthew 28:4 But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. Matthew 28:5 He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay. Matthew 28:6 Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you.” Matthew 28:7 So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples. Matthew 28:8 And behold, Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Matthew 28:9 Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” Matthew 28:10

title: Matthew 28:11–15
context: While the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests. The leaders bribe the soldiers to spread a theft story, promise protection from the governor, and a rival account takes root that Matthew says persists to his day.
text: Matthew 28:11–15 Matthew While the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests. The leaders bribe the soldiers to spread a theft story, promise protection from the governor, and a rival account takes root that Matthew says persists to his day. While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. Matthew 28:11 And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers Matthew 28:12 and said, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’ Matthew 28:13 And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” Matthew 28:14 So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day. Matthew 28:15

title: Matthew 28:16–20
context: The eleven meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee. They worship—yet some doubt. The risen Lord claims all authority in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all nations, commands Triune baptism and obedience-teaching, and promises His presence to the end of the age.
text: Matthew 28:16–20 Matthew The eleven meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee. They worship—yet some doubt. The risen Lord claims all authority in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all nations, commands Triune baptism and obedience-teaching, and promises His presence to the end of the age. Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. Matthew 28:16 And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted. Matthew 28:17 And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Matthew 28:18 Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Matthew 28:19 teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Matthew 28:20

title: Matthew 3:1–6
context: Years after the Nazareth settlement, Matthew jumps to John’s public ministry: a wilderness preacher calls Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, fulfills Isaiah’s voice, and baptizes confessing crowds in the Jordan.
text: Matthew 3:1–6 Matthew Years after the Nazareth settlement, Matthew jumps to John’s public ministry: a wilderness preacher calls Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, fulfills Isaiah’s voice, and baptizes confessing crowds in the Jordan. In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, Matthew 3:1 “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Matthew 3:2 For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” Matthew 3:3 Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. Matthew 3:4 Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, Matthew 3:5 and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. Matthew 3:6

title: Matthew 3:13–17
context: Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John; John hesitates, Jesus insists on fulfilling all righteousness, and after the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice names Jesus the beloved Son.
text: Matthew 3:13–17 Matthew Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John; John hesitates, Jesus insists on fulfilling all righteousness, and after the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice names Jesus the beloved Son. Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. Matthew 3:13 John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” Matthew 3:14 But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. Matthew 3:15 And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; Matthew 3:16 and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Matthew 3:17

title: Matthew 3:7–12
context: John confronts Pharisees and Sadducees seeking baptism without fruit: viper brood, Abrahamic presumption, axe at the root, and a Coming One who baptizes with Spirit and fire and separates wheat from chaff.
text: Matthew 3:7–12 Matthew John confronts Pharisees and Sadducees seeking baptism without fruit: viper brood, Abrahamic presumption, axe at the root, and a Coming One who baptizes with Spirit and fire and separates wheat from chaff. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Matthew 3:7 Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. Matthew 3:8 And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Matthew 3:9 Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Matthew 3:10 “I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. Matthew 3:11 His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” Matthew 3:12

title: Matthew 4:1–11
